segments.t: Continuing their talk in the kitchen, Dmitry Nagiyev reveals why tomorrow's guest matters so much: a famous producer is casting a new adaptation of War and Peace, and Nagiyev wants the role of Napoleon. Listen to their exchange in Russian.
Я тебя прошу, Витя, не облажайся.
Now let's go back through their exchange line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
'I can see by your eyes that you don't understand.' Notice how Russian puts 'see' and 'to understand' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'A film producer is coming.' Here Nagiyev anchors the thought on 'producer' and finishes on 'will arrive', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'He wants to film War and Peace.' In everyday Russian, 'wants' flows straight into 'world' without extra linking words.
'With me in the leading role.' Nagiyev pairs 'main, most important' with 'role, part' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
'I am going to play Napoleon.' Notice how Russian puts 'going' and 'to play' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'You have to feed him so well.' Here Nagiyev anchors the thought on 'so, like this' and finishes on 'to feed', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
Я тебя прошу, Витя, не облажайся.
'I am begging you, Vitya, don't mess this up.' Spoken Russian keeps this brief and expressive, built right around 'ask for' without extra helper words.
'Yes, got it.' Chef Barinov keeps this everyday Russian response short and direct, without needing English helper words like 'am', 'is', or 'are'.
'What did I just say?' Dmitry raises the pitch on the key word to turn this short Russian clause into a direct question.
'Onto the French throne.' Here Chef Barinov anchors the thought on 'French' and finishes on 'throne', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'I said do not mess it up.' Putting the short word for 'not' right in front of the action word is all Russian needs to make a sentence negative, with no extra helper words like 'do' or 'did'.
'Ah, that too.' Chef Barinov centers this short reply on 'also, too', letting a few direct words carry the whole meaning. Now let's hear the entire conversation once more from start to finish.
Я тебя прошу, Витя, не облажайся.
That finishes Nagiyev's grand Napoleon speech and his warning to Chef Barinov not to mess up the dinner. Pay attention to how Russian expresses future plans and urgent requests. Until next time!
